title: Framing the Bump for the Perfect Maternity Photo Pose
summary: Maternity photo poses for every trimester: where to put your hands, standing and seated options, and poses with a partner or older kids.
body_markdown:
## Finding the warmest pose for you and your baby


*Hands underneath rather than flat across the front. That keeps the shape, not hides it.*


You have spent months being told you are glowing by people who then photograph you from below, at a party, under a ceiling light. So when you finally book a session, the question is not whether you want the photos. It is what to do with your body once someone is actually pointing a camera at it.


Maternity posing is just as much mechanical as it is emotional. There is one thing in the frame that the whole photograph is about, and almost every rule follows from it. Give the bump a clean profile. Keep your arms off it. Put your hands where they frame rather than hide. The rest is comfort and light.


## When to book, and why timing changes the poses


*Unmistakable bump, comfortable on her feet. That is what the 28-to-34 week window buys.*


Somewhere between about 28 and 34 weeks is the usual window. The bump is unmistakable and you can still stand for a reasonable stretch.


Earlier and the side profile is not doing much work yet. Later and it becomes a seated session, which is fine but different. Carrying twins usually means moving the whole thing a few weeks earlier.


## Standing poses, and where your hands go


The side profile is the anchor. Turn fully side-on, then rotate your shoulders and face back toward the lens by about a quarter turn. Fully side-on with your face side-on too reads like a medical diagram. The turn back is what makes it a portrait.


The three-quarter turn is second. Angle your body away, weight onto the back foot, front knee soft. The bump keeps a visible edge and you get a waist back on one side.


Then the hand frame, which is most of the game. One hand cradles underneath the bump, the other rests higher on the side or top, so your forearms shape the subject instead of covering it. Two flat palms across the front is the default instinct and the pose that flattens the photograph: it hides the shape, presses your arms in and leaves nowhere for light to get through. Keep fingers soft and slightly separated rather than gripping, since a tense wrist reads as a tense person even at a distance.


## Seated and reclining poses


*Knees angled away, upper body turned back. That is what stops a seated frame going square.*


Sitting is not a compromise. Some of the best maternity frames are seated, because a lap changes how the bump reads.


On a chair or stool, sit toward the front edge, angle your knees away from the camera and turn your upper body back. Keeping the knees off-axis stops the frame going square and gives your hands somewhere natural to land.


Reclining works well late on. Lie on your side propped on a forearm and a cushion, top knee drawn up, top hand on the bump. If lying on your back makes you lightheaded, say so early and stay off it.


## Poses with a partner and older children


*Kissing the bump gives a small child a target.*


The wrap is the workhorse. Your partner stands behind you, arms around and under the bump, hands over yours. Look down at the bump for one frame and at the camera for the next.


The forehead touch is the second. Faces angled in, foreheads together, eyes closed, both sets of hands on the bump between you. It works at any height difference because contact happens at the top rather than the shoulders. Where there is a big gap, put the taller person on a lower step instead of asking anyone to stoop.


A toddler will not hold a pose, so plan a moment instead. Kissing the bump works because it gives a small child a target. Listening works for the same reason: an ear against the bump, eyes anywhere. Shoot these early while attention lasts, and keep the frames where nobody is looking at the camera.


## Comfort, and how long you can actually stand


Swelling builds through the day, so ankles are happier in the morning, but the light is better late. Most photographers compromise on the hours before sunset.


Bring flat shoes, and say out loud when a pose stops being comfortable. A good photographer would rather change it than keep a frame where your jaw is tight.


If you are outdoors, our notes on[the best and worst light for outdoor photos](https://www.snappr.com/blog/what-are-your-best-and-worst-options-to-get-the-best-light-for-your-outdoor-photos) will save you a bad hour. If you would rather be somewhere climate-controlled with a chair, the[studio rental guides](https://www.snappr.com/blog/top-5-photography-studios-for-rent-in-new-york-city) are a reasonable start.

## Frequently asked questions


### What week is best for maternity photos?


Most sessions land between 28 and 34 weeks, when the bump is clearly defined and standing is still comfortable. If you are expecting twins, book a few weeks earlier, since both the shape and the discomfort arrive sooner.


### Where do I put my hands in maternity photos?


One hand underneath the bump and one above or to the side. Two flat palms across the front covers the shape and presses your arms into your body, which flattens the frame. Keep fingers soft rather than gripping.


### What maternity poses work if I have back pain?


Seated and reclining ones. Sit toward the front edge of a chair with knees angled away from the camera, or lie on your side propped on a forearm with a cushion under the top knee. Tell your photographer early so the session is built around seated frames.


### What maternity poses work with a toddler?


Ones with a target rather than a held position. Kissing the bump and listening to the bump both give a small child a clear instruction. Shoot them early while attention lasts, and keep the frames where nobody looks at the camera.
